parole.testo: From Renaissance Latin Abyssīnī (“the Abyssinians”).

From Renaissance Latin Abyssīnī (“the Abyssinians”), from Arabic الْحَبَشَة (al-ḥabaša), from حَبَش (ḥabaš, “Abyssinian”). The humorous use of Abyssinia as a parting phrase is due to its phonetic resemblance to I'll be seeing ya.
From Renaissance Latin angulātiō. By surface analysis, angulate + -ion.
From de- + finitude or de- + Latin fin(is) + -itude, ultimately from Renaissance Latin finitūdō (“signifying a noun of state”), from fīnis (“end, limit”) + -tūdō.
From Renaissance Latin discarnatus, alteration of Classical Latin dēcarnātus. Compare decarnate.

parole.significato: To cause, bring about (an event); to accomplish, to carry out (a wish, plan etc.).
parole.testo: From the participle stem of Renaissance Latin effectuare, or its source, Latin effectus (“effect”); probably after Middle French effectuer.

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to Erasmus (Catholic priest and theologian).
parole.testo: From the Renaissance Latin Erasmiānus.

parole.significato: The state or characteristic of being finite; limitedness.
parole.testo: From Latin fin(is) + -itude or directly from Renaissance Latin finitūdō (“signifying a noun of state”), from fīnis (“end, limit”) + -tūdō.

Borrowed from Renaissance Latin flōrilegium, calque of Ancient Greek ἀνθολογία (anthología, “flower-gathering”) (compare English anthology), so called because flowers were used as symbols of the finer sensibility of literature.

parole.significato: The science that studies the structure of the Earth (or other planets), together with its origin and development, espec…
parole.testo: From geo- + -logy, partly after Renaissance Latin geōlogia, from Ancient Greek γεω- (geō-, “earth”) + Latin -logia (“the study of”), from Ancient Greek -λογία (-logía).

parole.significato: The quality of being indefinite or vague.
parole.testo: From in- + definitude, from in- + de- + Latin fin(is) + -itude or directly from Renaissance Latin finitūdō (“signifying a noun of state”), from fīnis (“end, limit”) + -tūdō.
From Renaissance Latin linguifōrmis, from Classical Latin lingua (“tongue”) + -fōrmis (“shaped”).

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to the theology of Martin Luther (1483–1546) or his followers, or the Lutheran church.
parole.testo: From the surname of German theologian and ecclesiastical reformer Martin Luther (1483–1546) + -an. Probably immediately from Renaissance Latin Lutheranus, or German Lutheraner. Calque of Renaissance Latin malum insanum, itself calqued from Italian melanzana, reanalyzed as if mela insana, perhaps under the influence of beliefs that it could cause various diseases. See further etymology at melongene.

parole.significato: Of or relating to the mamma or breast (of a woman or a female animal).
parole.testo: From Renaissance Latin mammārius, from Classical Latin mamma (“breast”) + -ārius (adjectival suffix). By surface analysis, mamma + -ary.
From Renaissance Latin multangulum, use as noun of neuter of Classical Latin multangulus.

parole.significato: The state or fact of being nothing; nothingness, nullity; nonexistence.
parole.testo: From Renaissance Latin nihilitās, from Latin nihil (“nothing”).

parole.testo: From Renaissance Latin polyanthus, corresponding to poly- + Ancient Greek ἄνθος (ánthos, “flower”).
From Renaissance Latin septangulāris. By surface analysis, sept- + -angular.
From septem- + -fid, after Renaissance Latin septemfidus.

parole.significato: A group of girls or women associated for a common purpose; a sisterhood.
parole.testo: PIE word  *swésōr From Renaissance Latin sorōritās, from Latin soror (“sister”), from Proto-Indo-European *swésōr. Akin to Spanish sororidad, Portuguese sororidade, French sororité.
